title: India Has Built Twenty Foundational AI Models. Five Are Already Live. The World Barely Noticed.
excerpt: The IndiaAI Mission is funding sovereign language models, video generators, and medical diagnostics AI — all designed to work in 22 Indian languages. The goal is not to beat OpenAI but to make sure India never depends on it.
body:
While the world's attention has been fixed on OpenAI, Anthropic, and the American AI arms race, India has been building something quieter — and potentially more consequential for the billion-plus people who speak its languages.

The IndiaAI Mission, backed by a ₹10,372 crore government allocation, has now funded the creation of 20 foundational AI models. Five have already been released to the public. And the ambition behind them is not to compete with Silicon Valley on benchmarks, but to ensure that the next generation of AI applications in India runs on Indian infrastructure, trained on Indian data, in Indian languages.

## The Models That Matter

Among the five released models, two stand out.

**Sarvam AI** has built a 105-billion-parameter model using a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with a 128,000-token context window. It is designed for complex reasoning tasks and supports all 22 official Indian languages — a capability that no frontier American model can match with equivalent fluency. The model is already available on AIKosh, the government's open-access AI platform, for developers to build applications.

**BharatGen**, led by an IIT Bombay consortium that received the largest government allocation at ₹1,058 crore, has produced a multimodal large language model spanning domains from Ayurveda and agriculture to law. Its scale ranges from 2 billion to 1 trillion parameters, and it too is live on AIKosh.

This week, Avataar.ai — one of 12 startups selected under the mission — launched **Varya**, India's first indigenous video AI model. Varya uses a distillation technique that compresses 50 processing steps into four, generating video at a fraction of the cost charged by global competitors like Runway and Luma. At ₹0.48 per second of video, Varya is roughly twenty times cheaper than comparable international offerings.

"For all those people who say that model making cannot succeed in India, this is an answer," said S. Krishnan, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, at the Varya launch.

## Not Just Models — Infrastructure

The more consequential shift is happening underneath the models, in the physical infrastructure required to train and run them.

Yotta Data Services announced a $2 billion project to deploy 20,736 liquid-cooled NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs — one of Asia's largest AI superclusters — at its Greater Noida campus, with a go-live date of August 2026. The deployment includes a four-year, $1 billion engagement with NVIDIA for one of the largest DGX Cloud clusters in the Asia-Pacific region. Over 10,000 GPUs from the supercluster will be committed to the IndiaAI Mission for sovereign model development.

"India is emerging as one of the world's most important AI markets," Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's CEO, said of the partnership. "Yotta's deployment creates advanced AI infrastructure capable of training frontier-scale models and delivering AI at population scale."

Separately, UrsaCompute has committed $300 million to deploy 2,888 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs across data centres in Greater Noida, Hyderabad, and Visakhapatnam. The company's pitch is blunt: AI leadership belongs not to whoever builds the best model, but to whoever owns the compute infrastructure beneath it.

## The Safety Layer

India has also launched the IndiaAI Safety Institute, a dedicated body to assess AI risks and promote responsible innovation. The institute's mandate includes evaluating models against global safety benchmarks while accounting for challenges specific to India's linguistic diversity and digital governance needs.

The timing is pointed. Anthropic, one of America's leading AI companies, saw its most advanced models suspended this week after the U.S. government issued an export control directive restricting foreign nationals' access — a move that would directly affect Indian engineers and enterprises using those models.

India's sovereign AI push is, at its core, an insurance policy against exactly this kind of dependency.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRI tech professionals — many of whom work at the very companies building America's AI stack — India's sovereign push creates a parallel opportunity. Sarvam AI, BharatGen, and Avataar.ai are all hiring. The GPU infrastructure boom is attracting private capital at a pace not seen since the telecom revolution of the early 2000s. And the models themselves, trained on Indian languages and cultural contexts, open application markets that global models simply cannot serve.

The 12 organisations funded by the mission — including Gnani AI, Soket AI, Tech Mahindra's Maker's Lab, and Fractal Analytics — represent a bet that India can build AI for itself, by itself. Whether that bet pays off will depend less on parameter counts than on whether Indian enterprises actually adopt these models over cheaper, more established American alternatives.

The next test comes in August, when Yotta's supercluster goes live and India gains the raw compute power to train models at a scale it has never attempted before.
